Attendance and participation at the City of La Verne Active Transportation & Infrastructure
Commission meetings are welcomed and appreciated. Community engagement provides the
Commission with valuable information. In compliance with the American Disabilities Act, any person
with a disability who requires a modification or accommodation in order to participate in a meeting
should contact the City Clerk’s Office at (909) 596-8726 at least 48 hours prior to the meeting.

Persons addressing the Active Transportation & Infrastructure Commission shall be limited to 3
minutes unless an extension of time is granted by the Chair, subject to approval of the Commission
Members. When any group of persons wishes to address the Commission, it shall be proper for the
Chair to request that a spokesperson be chosen to represent the group.

Public comments will be allowed on items on this Agenda at the time each item is considered.

Mission of the Active Transportation & Infrastructure Commission
To provide community-based advisory input to the City Council and Public Works Department on
capital projects, mobility, traffic safety, pavement management, and sustainable transportation
initiatives, helping prioritize infrastructure needs, promote multimodal access, and support informed
decision-making aligned with adopted plans and standards.

TO:  Honorable Chair and Commission Members
FROM:  Cody Howing, City Engineer
SUBJECT:  BOWDOIN STREET AND WILLIAMS AVENUE INTERSECTION CLOSURE

SUMMARY
The existing road closure on the west leg of the intersection of Bowdoin Street and Williams
Avenue was initiated in 1984 by the City Council to address concerns of bypass traffic in the
area. A landscaped median was constructed as a temporary condition to address the
congestion issues. Concerns from the community in the surrounding area were raised in 2021
as part of the comments received for Tract No. 83064. Following the completion of Tract No.
83064, the City is considering the future of the closure.

RECOMMENDATION
Receive and File.

DISCUSSION
In September 1984, the City Council adopted Resolution No. 84-76 to authorize the closure of
Bowdoin Street and Williams Avenue. This action was in response to traffic patterns from
vehicles seeking alternative routes to avoid a stop-controlled intersection at Baseline Road and
Williams Avenue. Notably, said intersection was also the local termination of Baseline Road as
it did not continue east beyond Williams Avenue at that time. The median was constructed
shortly after the decision by City Council and has remained in place to this day.

In May 2001, the item was brought back to City Council for consideration with completion of
Baseline Road improvements. The construction improvements of Baseline Road closed the
gap that had formerly existed between existing portions of roadway in La Verne and
Claremont. Williams Avenue was no longer the easterly termination point of Baseline Road In
the City of La Verne, allowing traffic connectivity between the existing segments on Baseline
Road. However, at that time, city staff had recommended to City Council that the closure at
Bowdoin Street and Williams Avenue remain closed until the completion of the SR-210 freeway.

In April of 2003, the item was brought back to City Council to consider the reopening of
Bowdoin Street at the intersection. The SR-210 freeway was nearing completion and was due
to open in the following months. A traffic study and community outreach followed that meeting
based on the City Council’s request for additional information. Results of a community survey
and traffic counts were brought back for the City Council’s consideration in May 2003. The
results of the 301 survey cards that were sent out yielded 125 responses opposed to opening
the intersection, 94 responses in support and five that did not submit an opinion. Further
community engagement was conducted based on City Council direction. Ultimately, in
December 2003, direction from City Council was issued that the closure should remain in

  Page 3 of 15
   Bowdoin Street and Williams Avenue Intersection Closure , Page 2

place.

In 2021, during the process of completing the Environmental Impact Report (EIR) for Tract No.
83064, comments from the community, including interest in removing the closure, were
received by the City. Although the closure was located to the north of the project and not
included in the scope of work, there was a statement noted in the Draft EIR that reopening the
intersection would benefit roadway operations. The project under review did not justify
reopening and further study of the intersection may be considered in the future.

On March 1, 2021, city staff brought to the City Council an item regarding the concept of
reopening the intersection. At that time, City Council gave direction for the subject be reviewed
with the Active Transportation Committee. Tract No. 83064 was ultimately approved and
construction was completed in June 2025.

Prior to the conclusion of construction for Tract No. 83064, city staff presented to the Active
Transportation Commission (ATC) in January 2025. In that presentation, background
information of the intersection closure and potential intersections for inclusion in a future traffic
study were considered. The approach was extended to the entire neighborhood to ensure all
the adjacent intersections were captured with both speeding and bypass traffic in mind for data
collection.

Also presented at that meeting were details of a settlement agreement between the original
developer for Tract No. 83064 and an unincorporated association identified as “Save Our La
Verne Environment” (SOLVE). The settlement agreement did not involve the City of La Verne
directly. However, features of that agreement between two private entities did involve the City
in the effect that $20,000 was to be paid by the original developer towards a traffic study the
City would oversee.

Following the feedback from ATC on the traffic study intersection scope, city staff requested
proposals from professional traffic engineering consultants to conduct a traffic study. The
resulting costs from two consultants that submitted proposals averaged approximately
$50,000. Given that the proposed consultant fees well exceeded the private funding for the
subject study, and that the undertaking is an optional feature the City is not mandated to
conduct, additional consideration was identified as due before initiating the
study. Coincidentally, the City of La Verne was in the process of reorganizing the public
advisory committees, resulting in the reconfiguration of the ATC to the Active Transportation
and Infrastructure Commission lending to that discussion being reviewed now.

The existing conditions of the intersection vary significantly from those that existed at the time
the closure was approved in 1984. Most notable is that Williams Avenue no longer connects to
Baseline Road and terminates south of the SR-210 freeway. The most recent changes to the
nearby neighborhood are from Tract No. 83064. A traffic study was conducted in 2021 for that
project, but did not include the Bowdoin Street and Williams Avenue intersection as it was
outside the project scope. Intersections that were affected by the project showed study results
of minor impacts from increased trips added to the roads with no changes to the Level of
Service (LOS) for the 2040 horizon year in the "build" and "no build" analysis.

A primary concern in the 1984 origination of the closure indicates pass-through traffic as a

  Page 4 of 15
   Bowdoin Street and Williams Avenue Intersection Closure , Page 3

source of the issues. Tract No. 83064 is a residential development and has not been observed
as a cause for added pass-through traffic to the surrounding neighborhood. The study
conducted in 2021 did identify that Vehicle Miles Traveled (VMT) for the project as a condition
that exceeded the allowable threshold and was not feasible to be addressed with mitigation
measures. While traffic related, VMT is a regional traffic measure with a focus on traffic
congestion and resulting greenhouse gas emissions for the purpose of compliance with the
California Environmental Quality Act. With respect to the subject intersection, LOS is a better
representation of the impacts on traffic at the local level.

In the interest of resolving the terms of the private party settlement agreement, the developer
has indicated willingness to contribute the $20,000 towards the cost of removing the closure in
lieu of applying the funds to a traffic study. Conducting a traffic study would require a
contribution of approximately $30,000 in city funds. Continued pursuit of a traffic study and
contribution of those city funds is a decision to be made by the City Council. However, should
the Active Transportation & Infrastructure Commission provide feedback on if the closure
should be removed or left in place, that information will be shared with the City Council when
the item is brought forward for consideration.

FISCAL ANALYSIS
There is no fiscal impact.

ENVIRONMENTAL ANALYSIS
Not applicable.

LEGAL REVIEW
Not applicable.

FROM:  Cody Howing, City Engineer
  Raymond Apodaca, Water Supervisor
SUBJECT:  UPDATE ON VARIOUS CAPITAL IMPROVEMENT PROJECTS

SUMMARY
The City of La Verne plans and implements various Capital Improvement Projects each
year. Information regarding active projects will be described.

RECOMMENDATION
Receive and File.

DISCUSSION
The City is currently in the process of implementing projects for Fiscal Year 2025-26. The
information described in this report represents Capital Improvement Projects that are subject to
transportation and infrastructure related scope of work.

Juanita Avenue and Damien Avenue Area Pavement Rehabilitation Project
This project is nearing design completion and is anticipated to be advertised for construction
bids in the coming weeks. The scope of work is focused on pavement resurfacing along
Juanita Avenue, Damien Avenue and the residential streets to the south and west of those two
noted streets. In addition to the resurfacing of the roadway, curb ramp, cross-gutter and
sidewalk repairs will be conducted.

White Avenue Pavement Rehabilitation Project
This project funding includes State Transportation Program Local (STPL) funds, which require
administrative processes for both design and construction involving Caltrans. The City recently
received approval of the project for the Preliminary Environmental Study in mid-April
2026. Prior to bidding the project for construction, the City must complete certification of Right-
of-Way and obtain authorization to bid the project from Caltrans prior to moving ahead with
construction. Completion of the remaining process requirements are expected to be submitted
to Caltrans by the end of April 2026.

Pending final approval from Caltrans to advertise for bidding of the project, city staff are
targeting a summer construction timeline for the work top be initiated. The work is focused on
rehabilitating the pavement surface of White Avenue from Foothill Boulevard to the vicinity of
Eighth Street. A sidewalk gap closure is also proposed on the east side of White Avenue
between Fifth Street and Sixth Street, along with pavement improvements to alleys east of
White Avenue.

  Page 8 of 15
   Update on Various Capital Improvement Projects, Page 2

Arrow Highway Urban Greening Project
This project is funded by a grant administered by the California Natural Resources Agency
(CRNA) for the purpose of installing landscaping improvements in existing raised medians
along Arrow Highway east of White Avenue. A construction contract was awarded by the City
Council in October 2025.

Work was conducted over a period of a few months and has recently been concluded. The
landscaping features included California native species. Notable features of the grant required
the City to plant trees no larger than 15-gallon sizing. A feature purpose of the grant funding is
to enhance carbon capture and sequestration. Utilizing younger planting material allows that to
be achieved. The total project budget, including design construction and contingencies, was
$529,465.

Fiscal Year 2025-26 CDBG Curb Ramp Improvement Project
The City of La Verne has received Community Development Block Grant funds. These funds
have a restricted use but are allowed to be spent on improvements that remove “architectural
barriers” in the public right-of-way. This year the City will be conducting a curb ramp and
sidewalk replacement project on portions of “A” Street and “C” Street. Intersection corners with
substandard or non-existent curb ramps will be updated with ADA complaint curb ramps. In
coordination with those improvements, areas of damaged sidewalk will also be replaced to
eliminate hazards.

A total of 16 bids were received by the City. The lowest bid submitted has been recommended
to City Council the award of a construction contract on the April 20, 2026 City Council
meeting. Construction is expected to commence in May 2026 and be completed prior to the
end of June 2026. The total project budget including contingencies is $140,618.

Plateau Forebay Transmission Pipeline Replacement Project
The Plateau Forebay Transmission Pipeline is a critical component of the City’s water system,
providing potable water supply, system pressure, and fire protection to residents in northern La
Verne (Zone 5). Identified as a priority in the City’s 2020 Water Master Plan, the project
addresses approximately 2,000 feet of aging 16-inch transmission main that has reached the
end of its service life. Due to the pipeline’s challenging hillside and canyon alignment, a hybrid
construction approach will be used, with lower segments replaced using open-trench installation
and ductile iron pipe, and the middle and upper segments rehabilitated using slip-lining to
minimize surface disturbance and reduce geotechnical risks. Other features in support of the
water main restoration include the installation of new valves and line stops to maintain system
operations during construction.

This project reflects the City’s ongoing reinvestment of water rate revenues into maintaining and
improving critical infrastructure. The total project budget is $3.5 million, including contingencies,
with construction anticipated to be completed by mid-August 2026.

SUBJECT:  PRELIMINARY DRAFT FY 2026/27 TO FY 2030/31 FIVE-YEAR CAPITAL
  IMPROVEMENT PROGRAM

SUMMARY
Presentation of the Preliminary Draft FY 2026/27 to 2030/31 Five-Year Capital Improvement
Program (CIP) to the Commission, to provide early visibility into the proposed CIP, and an
opportunity to offer input and feedback prior to formal consideration by the City Council.

RECOMMENDATION
Receive and File.

DISCUSSION
As part of the City's annual budget development process, the Public Works Department, in
coordination with other City Departments, updates the Capital Improvement Program
(CIP). The CIP presents an annual plan for the construction, rehabilitation, and replacement of
the City's infrastructure and public assets. The Preliminary Draft FY 2026/27 to 2030/31 Five-
Year CIP outlines the City’s proposed investments in infrastructure over the next five years,
including projects related to streets and sidewalks, storm drains, water and sewer systems,
facilities, parks, and landscaping. The CIP is a critical planning tool that aligns capital
investments with Council priorities and available funding sources.

Capital Improvement: A capital improvement is a major equipment acquisition or construction
project that usually requires expenditure of funds from sources other than normal operating
revenues. A capital improvement can be best described by citing common examples such as;
City Hall, Fire Station, Water and Sewer Facilities, Storm Drains, Park Land, Fire Trucks,
Computer Equipment, Traffic Signals, Right of Way Improvements and various other
infrastructure assets of the City.

Capital Improvement Program: A capital improvement program is a plan to authorize, acquire
or construct a number of capital improvements, according to a schedule over five years. The
CIP includes projects from all City departments and lists a description, justification, expected
cost, financing plan, tentative construction or acquisition dates and any other data thought
helpful, for each improvement.

Capital Budget: The capital improvement budget is a one-year, current budget of the
CIP. Funds for the FY 2026/27 capital program are specifically appropriated as provided by
law. Projects are more clearly defined, costed, and timed within the CIP document. The capital
improvement budget is adopted along with the City’s annual operating budget.

  Page 11 of 15
   Preliminary Draft FY 2026/27 to FY 2030/31 Five-Year Capital Improvement Program, Page 2

The Preliminary Draft FY 2026/27 to 2030/31 Five-Year CIP is currently under development as
part of the City’s annual budget process and continues to be refined as project scopes,
schedules, and funding assumptions are evaluated. The proposed program also requires final
review and approval by the City Manager prior to release. Subsequently, the CIP will be
presented to the Planning Commission for a General Plan consistency determination in May,
followed by City Council consideration and final adoption in June.

This presentation provides an early, high-level overview of the preliminary CIP, including
planned capital projects, anticipated funding sources, and overarching program
priorities. Emphasis is placed on maintaining and rehabilitating existing infrastructure,
addressing critical system needs, and aligning capital investments with available revenues,
grant opportunities, and long-term fiscal sustainability.

FISCAL ANALYSIS
There are no financial impacts based on the recommendations as all actions will be considered
as part of the Fiscal Year 2026-27 budget.

Not applicable.
